texts.orig: 1. How is the Miro product org structured?
texts.text: 1. How is the Miro product org structured?

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Over time, we’ve experimented with multiple organizational structures. The first structure divided the org between “Core Product” and “Growth,” which allowed each team to stay focused on one priority: delivering product features or driving growth. Then we evolved our structure to focus more on users, experimenting with use-case-focused teams to solve specific user needs and end-to-end experiences, e.g. Miro for workshops.

texts.orig: 2. How far out do you plan in detail, and how has that evolved over the years?
texts.text: 2. How far out do you plan in detail, and how has that evolved over the years?

texts.label: text
texts.orig: At the company level, we have a “three-year painted picture,” which is a high-level picture that Miro’s Leadership Team co-develops and that defines the outcomes we want to achieve—both for our users and for Miro as a company. The painted picture is bold and ambitious, and establishes a general direction for the entire company.

This phase is about building broad awareness and providing teams with clarity on what we want to do. We got (and answered) more than 1,000 questions in the most recent iteration and refined the details based on the team’s input.

The identified initiatives go into our product roadmap.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Our product roadmap operates on a rolling six-month cadence—we have 80% confidence in the current quarter and 50%-plus in the subsequent quarter. We used to plan just two weeks out, but this longer-term cadence allows us to be more strategic, while also being nimble and reacting to market changes. And we’ll revisit and update our product strategy mid-year based on the progress until then and the emerging market context.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: For example, Miro AI is in beta as of March 9, a point the team reached in just eight weeks. When changes are happening in the market or inside the company, you should be agile and ready to adjust, not trapped by your own planning. Our flexible roadmap framework allowed us to embrace this watershed moment in AI capabilities; we prioritized initiatives and secured a team that rapidly ideated, built, and deployed the features. Other key factors that helped us act fast included: people who had passion around the topic (a motivated team can do a lot!); singular focus, as we deprioritized everything else for the core AI team; and fast, almost daily iterations and standups where we tweaked things, resolved blockers, and highlighted achievements.

texts.orig: 3. Do you use OKRs in some form?
texts.text: 3. Do you use OKRs in some form?

texts.label: text
texts.orig: We do. And, like many other things, it is constantly evolving. We’ve improved a lot, but there’s also more work for us to do here.
texts.text: We do. And, like many other things, it is constantly evolving. We’ve improved a lot, but there’s also more work for us to do here.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: We used to have OKRs at each level in the organization: Company → AMPED → Product Stream → Team, and followed a quarterly planning process. It was great in theory but had many challenges.
texts.text: We used to have OKRs at each level in the organization: Company → AMPED → Product Stream → Team, and followed a quarterly planning process. It was great in theory but had many challenges.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: There were three big problems with this setup:
texts.text: There were three big problems with this setup:

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Overlapping initiatives:
texts.text: Overlapping initiatives:

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Having OKRs at every level meant each team had to define their objectives and initiatives. This often resulted in teams rephrasing the same initiative at different altitudes and adding it to many key results. It was hard to do traction (check execution against goals) and was not providing clarity or alignment for teams.
texts.text: Having OKRs at every level meant each team had to define their objectives and initiatives. This often resulted in teams rephrasing the same initiative at different altitudes and adding it to many key results. It was hard to do traction (check execution against goals) and was not providing clarity or alignment for teams.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: So we’ve removed extra layers and now have Company-, AMPED-, and Product Stream-level OKRs, with each team just deciding which OKRs they will support. It has brought much-needed alignment and clarity to teams.
texts.text: So we’ve removed extra layers and now have Company-, AMPED-, and Product Stream-level OKRs, with each team just deciding which OKRs they will support. It has brought much-needed alignment and clarity to teams.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Too much time for the “process”:
texts.text: Too much time for the “process”:

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Quarterly planning needs a lot of time. In addition, the same DRIs had to present updates at multiple traction forums. It led to a lot of time being spent in following the process and was just not working.
texts.text: Quarterly planning needs a lot of time. In addition, the same DRIs had to present updates at multiple traction forums. It led to a lot of time being spent in following the process and was just not working.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: So we’ve moved to a semi-annual OKR frequency and fewer OKR tractions each month, reducing duplicate and process-related work by a lot. We also do quarterly check-ins for course correction, if needed. For example, if a KR metric is no longer relevant, or based on rolling forecasts, we need to adjust targets.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Too many priorities:
texts.text: Too many priorities:

texts.label: text
texts.orig: We were seeing approximately three to five objectives with three to four KRs per objective. At each level, we created new sets of metrics, dashboards, and monthly traction reports, making it difficult to get a comprehensive overview of our common priorities. It was clear we weren’t driving focus.
texts.text: We were seeing approximately three to five objectives with three to four KRs per objective. At each level, we created new sets of metrics, dashboards, and monthly traction reports, making it difficult to get a comprehensive overview of our common priorities. It was clear we weren’t driving focus.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: So we’ve started limiting the number of objectives and KRs (three to four objectives, two to three KRs) to start focusing from the top. This is still a work in progress, and we’ll continue to sharpen the pencil here.
texts.text: So we’ve started limiting the number of objectives and KRs (three to four objectives, two to three KRs) to start focusing from the top. This is still a work in progress, and we’ll continue to sharpen the pencil here.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Today we represent our OKRs as a ladder framework, where companywide OKRs are the most encompassing, followed by AMPED, and then the Stream, to avoid duplication. We also reduced the set of metrics that we track. The Product stream leaders present these to me as Chief Product Officer and to our CTO, Vadim Barshtak, for review and sign-off. We have an AMPED-wide monthly traction meeting where we discuss the most important topics and try to address the challenges that we see.

texts.orig: We spend about five hours per week on product review meetings for large initiatives. These reviews are cross-functional, and the AMPED product team presents together (not just the product managers). These reviews are open to everyone, but, to ensure it’s highly relevant and to reduce cost, we identify and ensure the participation of critical stakeholders who are needed to make decisions (e.g. DRIs as well as Product leaders, who can veto or provide specific direction). At the time of booking a slot, the Product team identifies who needs to be present and the Product Excellence team that runs the reviews tries to ensure their participation.

texts.orig: 8. How does your team estimate work items, track velocity, and know when something’s off track?
texts.text: 8. How does your team estimate work items, track velocity, and know when something’s off track?

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Miro’s Product organization is a constellation of autonomous teams, empowered to solve a business problem end-to-end. They leverage that autonomy to develop ways of working that enable them to succeed in their particular problem space. We don’t enforce a common system to do this.
texts.text: Miro’s Product organization is a constellation of autonomous teams, empowered to solve a business problem end-to-end. They leverage that autonomy to develop ways of working that enable them to succeed in their particular problem space. We don’t enforce a common system to do this.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Our product development lifecycle consists of a number of phases. At the end of the first phase (the P0 phase we mentioned above), teams use relative estimation techniques—such as planning poker, Pomodoro, affinity estimation, or T-shirt sizing—to align on a rough timeline.

texts.orig: 9. How do you, as a product leader and product team, balance resources between new product work vs. maintenance/bugs? Is there a general rule of thumb or system, or is it ad hoc and team-specific?
texts.text: 9. How do you, as a product leader and product team, balance resources between new product work vs. maintenance/bugs? Is there a general rule of thumb or system, or is it ad hoc and team-specific?

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Our general rule of thumb is to devote 60% of resources to product innovation, 20% to running the business (RTB, maintenance, and bugs), and the final 20% to tech innovation (reducing tech debt).
texts.text: Our general rule of thumb is to devote 60% of resources to product innovation, 20% to running the business (RTB, maintenance, and bugs), and the final 20% to tech innovation (reducing tech debt).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: That said, this balance depends on the maturity of the product. So if there are a lot of legacy issues, then tech debt requires more than 20%; or, if we’re shipping a new capability, product innovation is closer to 80%.
texts.text: That said, this balance depends on the maturity of the product. So if there are a lot of legacy issues, then tech debt requires more than 20%; or, if we’re shipping a new capability, product innovation is closer to 80%.

texts.orig: which started as a small experiment within the Product organization for teams to get together and showcase the cool stuff they’ve been working on. If I am in the office when Miro Connect is happening, I never miss attending because it’s so great to experience the energy.
